data.title: Extreme Networks Shares Jump on Report of Sale Process
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall

Shares of Extreme Networks rose after Reuters reported that the networking software and equipment company is exploring a sale.

Shares were up 13% at $23.70 on Friday. The stock has gained 42% this year.

The company has engaged an investment bank for a sale process, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Possible strategic buyers could be Fortinet, Cisco and NetApp, according to the report.

Extreme Networks and NetApp declined to comment to Reuters, while Cisco and Fortinet didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Write to Elias Schisgall at elias.schisgall@wsj.com

data.title: Microsoft winds down rented AI computing capacity from Oracle: report
data.description:
Key points:
  • Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle , Bloomberg News reported on Friday.
  • Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to the report.
  • The computing capacity had become less useful because it no longer met Microsoft's requirements. The Oracle servers used older-generation Nvidia chips, the people said.
  • The agreement, announced in 2023, involved Oracle providing Microsoft access to servers that would power a new AI-assisted version of its Bing search engine. The full value of the deal is not public.
  • Microsoft also decided against expanding its computing agreement with British AI cloud provider Nscale at a Texas data center. The potential extension would have been worth tens of billions of dollars to Nscale .
  • Microsoft has been taking a more cautious approach to renting computing capacity from third-party AI providers, amid concerns about project delays, regulatory hurdles, and rising costs. The company is also directing more spending toward expanding its data center capacity.

data.title: IDBI Bank stake sale: 'Very, very remote' chance of finding another buyer at Rs.52,000 crore, says DIPAM Secretary Chawla
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 6 -- The government opted to continue with the IDBI Bank disinvestment exercise by giving bidders another opportunity to improve their offers, rather than abandoning the existing process, DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla said. He clarified that the reserve price remained unchanged throughout the exercise.

During a conversation with CNBC-TV18, Chawla described the chances of attracting a fresh buyer prepared to pay Rs.52,000 crore for the combined government and Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) stakes as "very, very remote".

He stated the authorities weighed three alternatives - cancelling the initial bidding exercise, accepting the offer already received, and inviting improved bids - before the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD) settled on seeking revised or best offers to maximise the transaction value.

Chawla explained that the subsequent bidding exercise differed from the initial round because all parties involved were already aware of the price discovered during the first phase.

He said strategic disinvestment deals are not conducted like regular auctions with a fixed reserve-price threshold against which every bid is evaluated.

Rejecting the view that offers below the reserve price are automatically ineligible for approval, Chawla pointed to the Paradeep Phosphates privatisation, where the accepted offer was 15% lower than the reserve price.

He further said the revised offer exceeded the fair-value assessments as well as their average. The Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD) unanimously considered the improved bid reasonable, he added.

Chawla said the government introduced an income-tax indemnity capped at Rs.627 crore for the bidders, a provision that contributed to a Rs.3,917-crore increase in the bid value.

He mentioned the decision was based on the overall financial gains expected to accrue to the government and LIC from the transaction, rather than viewing the reserve price as a rigid benchmark.

Chawla reiterated that the reserve price remained unchanged throughout the bidding exercise and was neither revised nor fixed again.

On October 14, the government cleared the proposed sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Canada-based Fairfax Financial Holdings for approximately Rs.53,000 crore ($5.5 billion). The deal, if completed, would mark the largest foreign investment in an Indian bank and a significant step forward in the country's long-pending banking privatisation programme.

The strategic disinvestment is targeted for completion by the end of the current financial year, subject to regulatory approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

data.title: US FAA administrator to testify on $12.5 billion air traffic overhaul
data.description:
Key points:
  • Trump administration seeks another $30 billion for towers, software, digital upgrades and airport facilities
  • FAA plans to replace floppy disks at more than 400 facilities by end-2028
  • Government report says Congress must approve more money to finish program's first phase

By David Shepardson

The head of the Federal Aviation Administration will testify next week before a House of Representatives panel on the ongoing $12.5 billion effort to modernize the aging US air traffic control system, congressional aides said on Friday.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford will update the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on Tuesday on progress and ongoing challenges as it works to replace ancient equipment like copper telecom lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track airplanes.

Congress approved $12.5 billion over five years in June 2025 for air traffic control reforms but the Trump administration wants another $30 billion for air traffic control towers, software ‌and digital upgrades as well as improving airport facilities.

It's unclear if Congress will approve more money this year. Democrats are set to take control in January after big wins in this week's midterm elections.

Major airlines including American Airlines, Delta Air Lines , United Airlines and Southwest Airlines strongly back the $30 billion Trump administration proposal.

MORE MONEY NEEDED

A recent government report said Congress needs to approve more money just to finish the first phase of the air traffic control program and that the FAA needs a better estimate of how much the new system will cost to operate.

The FAA relies on telecoms systems it is racing to replace as well as decades-old Compaq computers and replacement parts bought on eBay. The US has the world's most ​complex airspace and faces a shortage ⁠of several thousand air traffic controllers.

The FAA said on Thursday it would replace by the end of 2028 the outdated floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities across the country.

In September, thousands ​of US flights were delayed or canceled due to the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia air ‌traffic facility and the accidental severing of a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew.

The FAA has also been working for years to end a long-ridiculed, decades-old practice of air traffic controllers using paper flight strips to keep track of aircraft by 2028. A total of 27 major airports have already done away with the paper strips.

data.title: In Republican collapse, Colorado military town elects Democrat for the first time
data.description:
Key points:
  • Army vet Killin becomes first Democrat to win district created in 1970
  • Unaffiliated voters swell to 53% of El Paso County electorate, county data shows
  • Killin outraised her Republican opponent

By Andrew Hay and Brad Brooks

Colorado Springs, a military town and global center for Christian evangelism, has sent a Republican to Washington every election since its US House of Representatives district was created in 1970.

Then came 2026.

The victory of Jessica Killin, an Army veteran who was among dozens of Democrats who flipped a seat this week, is one of the starkest examples of how the party built its resounding win on affordability issues, demographics and candidates, one district at a time.

In an area with five military installations, where soldiers pack fast-food restaurants at lunchtime, Killin's triumph relied on votes of veterans, service members and their families, who represent about a third of the population, and for whom the war in Iran is personal. A soldier deployed from the city's Fort Carson US Army base was among the first Americans to die in the conflict.

Killin, a first-time candidate, said her win was a repudiation of Republican incumbent Jeff Crank's support for President Donald Trump and underscored voters' frustrations with the Iran war, tariffs and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

A supporter who canvassed for her found immigration also was on the minds of Latinos in a district where the population of metropolitan Colorado Springs more than doubled to around 782,000 in the last four decades, bringing greater ethnic diversity and a younger, more highly educated electorate.

"I am resolved to make the history that really matters, combating horrific corruption and chaos that we are all honestly sick of in Washington, DC," Killin, a former US Army paratrooper and aide to ex-second gentleman Doug Emhoff, told reporters on Thursday.

Crank had tried to portray Killin as an outsider.

"We cannot let our community turn into Denver or Boulder," Crank posted on social media last week, referring to the two Democratic-controlled cities to the north.

Killin targeted centrist and left-leaning residents in the state’s second-largest city, and her hometown, who in the past three presidential cycles abandoned both major parties, swelling unaffiliated voters by nearly half to 53% of the electorate in El Paso County, according to county data.

In a metropolitan area where more than 200 space, aerospace, cybersecurity, and defense companies employ around 111,000 people, and account for over 40% of the local economy, Killin hammered Crank's support of Trump's "reckless" war in Iran and argued that Congress needed to reclaim its war-powers authority.

Karl Schneider, 57, a former US special forces officer and ex-chair of the El Paso Republican Party, backed Killin to rein in a presidency he sees as militarily out of control.

"Donald Trump is a clear and present danger to the United States of America, our republic, and I think to the rest of the world," said Schneider, an executive at an AI cybersecurity advisory firm who served as a US Army Green Beret.

For others, like Rick Wood, 67, Crank failed to help tackle high gas and grocery prices and tied himself too closely to Trump, whose approval rating is near a career low of 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos national poll.

"They ran on Trump's coattails," said Wood, a US Air Force veteran.

'NEVER SEEN BEFORE'

Some Republicans interviewed by Reuters in the district that is home to the Focus on the Family evangelical organization were stunned by the blue wave, saying they feared the country would descend into communism, echoing warnings from Trump about the recent rise of left-wing Democratic candidates.

Politics professor Sara Hagedorn saw Killin, and other Democrats who won in former Republican strongholds, as a possible return to the fiscally responsible "Blue Dog" Democrats of the 1990s and early 2000s who worked across party lines.

"She has a real opportunity here to be a real moderate or independent voice within the Democratic Party," said Hagedorn, who teaches at the University of Colorado, Colorado Springs.

Killin's campaign coffers swelled after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed the district as "in play" in February, the first time the committee had targeted the area.

Bruce Barron, 65, a former Republican congressional aide, canvassed for Killin in southeast Colorado Springs where the school district has around 54% Hispanic students and many of the Black community live.

"Every Hispanic I talked to, it resonates with them, the concern about Hispanics not being safe under the Trump administration,” said Barron.

Killin’s campaign outraised Crank’s by nearly two to one with $5.6 million in funds.

She deployed over 400 volunteers to knock on over 100,000 doors while hosting around 150 events to meet voters, according to the campaign.

As Kyle Trei, 40, canvassed for Killin in south Colorado Springs, where American flags fly outside many homes and fuel-hungry pickups stand in driveways, he met conservatives willing to support Killin after they saw Crank back a war that has stoked energy prices.

"This is a candidate that this district has never seen before," Trei, an IT professional, said of Killin.

data.title: Gold drops 1% as strong US payrolls boost dollar, yields
data.description:
Key points:
  • US job growth beats expectations in October
  • Bullion on track for best week since late August
  • Price dip spurs gold buying in India ahead of Diwali
  • Silver, platinum and palladium head for weekly gains

By Anushree Mukherjee

Gold prices fell 1% on Friday after stronger-than-expected US payrolls data reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve could keep interest rates higher for longer, boosting the dollar and Treasury yields.

Spot gold fell 0.6% to $4,062.11 per ounce by 12:35 p.m. ET (1734 GMT). The metal fell by more than 1% to hit a low of $4,033.29 earlier in the session.

Spot gold was up 4.8% for the week, on track for its best week since August.

US gold futures for December delivery dropped 1% to $4,071.30.

The US dollar rose 0.7% to its highest level since October 29, making dollar-denominated gold more expensive for holders of other currencies, while benchmark 10-year Treasury yields also climbed.

"Gold gapped lower on a stellar employment report (that was) strong across the board, but is trying to claw back higher. This is a litmus test for this week's rally," independent metals trader Tai Wong said.

US nonfarm payrolls increased more than expected in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting the labor market remained resilient and giving the Federal Reserve more scope to focus on inflation stemming from the Middle East conflict.

Traders currently see an 81% chance that the Fed will raise rates in December, compared with 72.8% before the payrolls report, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, making gold less attractive to investors.

Brent crude was on track for a sharp weekly drop on expectations of a de-escalation in the US-Iran war after midterm election results, although persistent Middle East supply concerns continued to support prices.

Two Federal Reserve officials on Thursday backed small, steady rate hikes to rein in above-target inflation.

On the physical front, lower gold prices encouraged Indian retail buying ahead of the key Diwali festival. Gold had dropped to a one-year low of $3,869.85 an ounce on October 30.

Among other metals, spot silver rose 0.3% to $51.93, platinum gained 1.6%, while palladium fell 1% to $1,020.75. All three were poised for weekly gains.

data.title: CBC Pensioners Association Welcomes CBC Funding but Says Federal Budget Falls Short for Seniors
data.description:
(TheNewswire)

    November 6, 2026 – TheNewswire - The CBC Pensioners Association welcomes the federal government's announcement of an additional $300 million over two years for CBC/Radio-Canada in Budget 2026. However, the Association says the investment does little to address the longer-term funding challenges facing Canada's public broadcaster and falls short of the government's commitment during the last federal election to work toward bringing CBC/Radio-Canada's funding in line with the average funding of other national public broadcasters.

    "We are pleased to see additional funding for CBC/Radio-Canada. It is an important recognition of the role our public broadcaster plays in Canadian society," said Dan Oldfield, President of the CBC Pensioners Association. "However, a two-year funding commitment does not provide the long-term stability and predictability that CBC/Radio-Canada needs to fulfil its mandate and plan for the future."

    The Association recognizes that Canada's economic and political circumstances have changed considerably since last spring's federal election. Nevertheless, it is concerned that the government's longer-term commitment to strengthening public broadcasting has not been accompanied by a clear funding framework or a plan to achieve funding levels comparable to those of other G7 public broadcasters.

    The Association is also deeply disappointed by the lack of meaningful, broad-based measures addressing the financial security and well-being of Canada's seniors.

    Canadians aged 65 and older now represent approximately one-fifth of the population, a proportion projected to grow to nearly one-quarter over the coming decades. Yet Budget 2026 offers little in the way of a comprehensive response to the needs of this growing segment of the population.

    While the Association recognizes the value of measures such as the expanded Canada Caregiver Credit and the additional Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit supplement, these are targeted initiatives that will not address the broader financial pressures facing the majority of retirees.

    "Older Canadians have contributed to this country throughout their working lives and continue to make important contributions to their families and communities," said Oldfield. "They deserve more than a collection of targeted measures. They deserve a comprehensive approach to retirement income security and access to essential health care."

    The Association is particularly concerned about the absence of meaningful action on issues such as retirement income adequacy, access to affordable dental care and prescription medications. These are not peripheral concerns for older Canadians. They have a direct impact on their financial security and quality of life.

    The CBC Pensioners Association will continue to press the federal government on these issues. Representatives of the Association will be meeting with Members of Parliament and government policy-makers on Parliament Hill in the coming weeks to raise concerns about the future of public broadcasting and the need for a stronger federal commitment to Canada's seniors.

    The Association believes that a country that values its public institutions must also value the people who helped build them. Both Canada's public broadcaster and its growing senior population deserve meaningful, long-term commitments from the federal government.

    About the CBC Pensioners Association

    The CBC Pensioners Association represents retired employees of CBC/Radio-Canada. The Association works to protect and advance the interests of its members, maintain a constructive relationship with CBC/Radio-Canada and advocate on issues affecting pensioners and Canada's public broadcaster.

    For more information, contact communications@cbcpensioners.ca.

data.title: Under Armour flags broad-based weakness, sees steeper-than-expected third-quarter sales decline
data.description:
Under Armour on Friday flagged weakness across its portfolio, as the athletic apparel maker grapples with a challenging consumer environment and aggressive discounting by competitors clearing inventory.

The company also cut its annual gross margin forecast, saying Middle East-related disruptions had extended beyond its previous expectations, adding to pressure from elevated fuel and freight costs.

Shares of the company, which plunged about 12% premarket, were down about 3%.

Here are some details:

  • The company reported declines across all major product categories in the second quarter, led by an about 11% drop in footwear sales, while apparel fell 6% and accessories about 7%.

  • It now expects third-quarter revenue to decline about 8% to 9%; analysts expected a fall of about 4%, according to data compiled by LSEG

  • It also sees adjusted loss of one to three cents in the quarter, well below expectations of four cent profit

  • The company expects annual gross margin to increase 170 to 220 basis points, slower than its prior view of a 220 to 270 basis-point improvement

  • Under Armour forecasts low double-digit decline in the third-quarter in North America, a major revenue contributor

  • Current traffic and macroeconomic pressures could result in North America declining more than previously anticipated this fiscal year, CFO Reza Taleghani said on a post-earnings call

  • Under Armour's second-quarter revenue and adjusted earnings per share edged past expectations

  • "Under Armour is making progress on simplifying the business, cutting costs, and upgrading its products, but there's a long way to go," Morningstar analyst David Swartz said, adding that the company's turnaround remains challenged by weak industry demand, widespread promotional activity and high gas prices

  • Under Armour forecast a roughly $45 million impact from the Middle East conflict, up from the prior view of $35 million
